evals.prompt: Define generative qualitative user research in 2-3 sentences. Name its core method families and when it is typically done.
expected_elements: Learning what real people do, think, feel, and need in their own context — typically before a solution exists
Names method families: generative interviews, contextual methods (contextual inquiry, observation, shadowing), and longitudinal methods (diary studies, experience sampling)
States it is generative (discover needs/context), distinct from evaluating an existing artifact
Studies real users, not assumptions or imagined users

evals.prompt: Why does user research lean on 'tell me about the last time you…' rather than 'would you use…' questions?
expected_elements: People are unreliable narrators of their own future/hypothetical behavior but reliable about concrete recent episodes
Episodic memory is more trustworthy than self-prediction
Hypothetical/future-tense questions invite speculation, not evidence
Anchoring on a real past event yields verifiable behavior rather than imagined behavior

evals.prompt: Compare contextual inquiry, fly-on-the-wall observation, and shadowing. What does each trade off?
expected_elements: Contextual inquiry: master-apprentice stance, researcher asks clarifying questions while the user works — more depth, more intrusion
Fly-on-the-wall: removes researcher questions entirely — most naturalistic, least interpretive depth
Shadowing: follows a single user through their day
The core trade-off is naturalism (less intrusion → more authentic behavior) vs depth (more questions → richer interpretation)

evals.prompt: You are writing an interview guide. What construction rules keep it from producing biased data?
expected_elements: Open with broad context questions, then move to specific recent episodes
Avoid hypotheticals ('would you use…') and leading/solution-prompting questions ('don't you find it frustrating…')
Use silence and 'say more about that' rather than paraphrasing or finishing sentences
Use critical-incident technique and 5 Whys laddering to push past surface answers

evals.prompt: A behavior unfolds over weeks (how someone manages a chronic condition day to day). Which method fits and why?
expected_elements: A diary study / longitudinal method, because the behavior does not surface in a single session
Daily prompts, photo diaries, or experience sampling capture in-context moments
Reduces recall bias by capturing the moment rather than relying on later memory
A single interview would miss the day-to-day variation

evals.prompt: A team has a working prototype and asks user-research to check whether users can complete the checkout flow on it. Is that in scope? Why or why not?
expected_elements: Not in scope — that is usability-testing (evaluative: watching users attempt tasks on an existing artifact to find defects)
User research is generative — it studies users before an artifact exists, to discover needs and context
Correctly distinguishes generative discovery from evaluative testing
Redirects to usability-testing rather than answering out of lane

evals.prompt: A stakeholder says 'just ask users what features they want and build the top ones.' Correct the mental model.
expected_elements: People cannot reliably predict their own future behavior or preferences
Asking for desired features yields speculation and solution-prompting, not evidence of real need
Better: ask about concrete recent episodes and observe behavior, since what people do and say they do differ
Research uncovers needs and context, which the team translates into solutions — users do not hand over the answer

evals.prompt: After a round of interviews, how do you verify the research was sound rather than self-confirming?
expected_elements: The guide contained no leading/hypothetical/solution-prompting questions; every question answerable by a real past event
At least one finding contradicts a hypothesis the team held going in (if all findings confirm, questions were probably leading)
Sessions recorded with consent so synthesis works from primary data, not memory
Sample composition documented including who was excluded and why; for contextual studies, observation in the real environment
The researcher can name what they still don't know, not just what they confirmed
